values.label: Background repository configuration updates
values.description: Apply recommended repository configuration changes asynchronously after installation.

clusters.name: Packfile Lifecycle Management
clusters.description: How packfiles are consolidated, indexed, redirected, and deleted without exhausting file handles or disrupting foreground Git operations.

values.label: Incremental small-batch repacking
values.description: Rewrites bounded batches of small packfiles instead of attempting unlimited or repository-wide repacking.

values.label: Multi-pack-index object relocation
values.description: Uses the multi-pack-index to redirect objects into newly created packs while avoiding reads from superseded packs.

values.label: Two-phase consolidation and expiration
values.description: Separates pack creation and reference updates from deletion so cleanup occurs only after old packs are unreferenced.

values.label: Deferred unreferenced-pack deletion
values.description: Retains old packs until their objects have been redirected and no references remain.

values.label: Foreground-command continuity
values.description: Designs maintenance so foreground Git commands continue operating during repacking and expiration.

values.label: Unbounded packfile growth
values.description: Allows pack counts to grow without bound, creating file-handle scalability problems.

values.label: Pack-count and storage reduction
values.description: Deployment reduced repositories from thousands of packs and 150–200 GB to fewer than 100 packs and 30–50 GB.

values.label: Loose-object cleanup
values.description: Maintenance removes accumulated loose objects to reduce storage and lookup overhead.

values.label: Single-pack full repacking
values.description: All repository data is rewritten into one packfile to reduce lookup overhead.

values.label: Pack-index accumulation lookup cost
values.description: Accumulating packfiles increases the number of indexes Git must inspect and slows object lookup.

values.label: Background incremental repository maintenance
values.description: Perform repository cleanup and rewriting incrementally in background processes rather than blocking foreground commands.

values.label: Foreground automatic garbage collection
values.description: Run complete automatic garbage collection synchronously at the end of user commands.

values.label: Foreground garbage-collection blocking
values.description: Foreground garbage collection blocks commands and can exhaust CPU and memory during repository rewrites.

values.label: Performance decay from disabled automatic collection
values.description: Avoid foreground collection but allow accumulated objects to gradually degrade Git performance.

values.label: Primary-only compaction scheduling
values.description: Schedule repository compaction on only the primary replica and propagate its results to peers.

values.label: WAL-propagated compaction events
values.description: Propagate compaction results through the WAL so replicas apply the same repository maintenance events.

values.label: S3 distribution of compacted packs
values.description: Distribute already-compacted packs from object storage instead of repacking independently on replicas.

values.label: Periodic write-ahead-log compaction
values.description: Compact the WAL periodically to bound restoration work as updates accumulate.

values.label: On-disk layout optimization for compaction
values.description: Optimize repository disk layout to reduce compaction impact on ingestion.

values.label: Compaction-limited push throughput
values.description: Push throughput becomes bounded by on-disk compaction speed after WAL latency is reduced.

values.label: Replica-local repository repacking
values.description: Repack repositories independently on each replica.

values.label: Replica failover from concurrent maintenance
values.description: Concurrent compaction on replicas can trigger repository failover and reduce availability.

values.label: Automatic Git garbage-collection disablement
values.description: Disable foreground automatic garbage collection and shift cleanup to background maintenance.

clusters.name: Repository Replication Layer
clusters.description: Which system layer and mechanism performs repository replication across hosts.

relations.reading: Repository Replication Layer affects Replica Write Coordination Strategy
relations.rationale: The new documents state that geographic replica distance adds latency and constrains reference-update throughput.

relations.reading: Repository Replication Layer affects Replica Write Coordination Strategy
relations.rationale: The new documents state that geographic replica distance adds latency and constrains reference-update throughput.

values.label: DRBD block-level replication
values.description: Replication is performed below the application at the filesystem block level.

values.label: Co-located replica placement
values.description: Replicas are kept physically close to satisfy block-replication latency constraints.

values.label: Application-level Spokes replication
values.description: An application-level system replicates Git repositories and manages their copies across file servers.

values.label: Distant replica placement
values.description: Replicas are deliberately distributed across greater geographic distances despite added latency.

values.label: Git-and-rsync replication
values.description: Replication combines Git-aware operations with rsync for copying, repair, and rebalancing.

values.label: S3-backed write-ahead-log authority
values.description: Authoritative repository state is retained in durable object storage while hosts serve reconstructible working copies.

values.label: WAL-based repository provenance and replica rewind
values.description: The authoritative log records repository operations so states can be reconstructed, rewound, and fast-forwarded.

values.label: Optimistic UDP gossip replication
values.description: Exchange replica catch-up metadata through lossy gossip while retaining authoritative recovery from the WAL.

values.label: ETag-validated replica freshness
values.description: Validate replica currency against the WAL index before serving reads.

values.label: WAL-index catch-up before reads
values.description: Catch replicas up from a newer WAL index before serving fetches or clones.

values.label: S3-backed globally consistent reads
values.description: Use authoritative S3 state checks so replicas expose a consistent repository view despite message loss or topology changes.

values.label: Arbitrary replica-count scaling
values.description: Scale read-serving capacity by deploying an arbitrary number of consistent replicas.

values.label: Fully consistent replica cluster
values.description: Maintain full consistency across replicas while adding read and RPC serving capacity.

values.label: WAL-first storage design
values.description: Use the write-ahead log as the primary durability and replication foundation for repository updates.

values.label: S3 Express One Zone WAL storage
values.description: Use low-latency S3 Express One Zone as the WAL persistence layer for high push rates.

values.label: Batched WAL operations
values.description: Batch WAL writes to reduce object-store latency and sustain high push ingestion rates.

values.label: Low-latency replica placement
values.description: Place replicas close enough to sustain high-rate update coordination.

values.label: Single-S3-write-per-push model
values.description: Persist each push with one object-store write.

clusters.name: Repository Hosting Model
clusters.description: Which collaboration and hosting model combines client decentralization with repository service centralization?

values.label: Distributed version-control model
values.description: Clients retain decentralized version-control capabilities while collaborating through hosted repositories.

values.label: Centralized repository hosting
values.description: Organizations rely on a central host for shared repository collaboration despite distributed client capabilities.

values.label: Hybrid distributed-client centralized-host architecture
values.description: Distributed client workflows such as offline work and delayed pushes operate against centralized repository hosting.

values.label: Git repository hosting difficulty
values.description: Hosting Git repositories creates substantial scalability and operational complexity.

values.label: Distributed Git implementation
values.description: The hosting system itself distributes or modifies Git rather than retaining standard Git as the implementation boundary.

clusters.name: Repository Cache Materialization Strategy
clusters.description: How repository state is cached, discarded, and reconstructed to balance local responsiveness, storage cost, and materialization work.

values.label: Local-disk repository warm cache
values.description: Hosts keep repositories as local working copies for efficient access without making local placement authoritative.

values.label: On-demand repository materialization
values.description: A missing repository is reconstructed from authoritative log state on the host that needs to serve it.

values.label: Idle-replica disk garbage collection
values.description: Remove inactive repository replicas from local disk to reduce retained storage.

values.label: On-demand replica rematerialization
values.description: Reconstruct an evicted repository replica from the WAL when demand returns.

iterations.explanation: Added batch evidence to existing dimensions; added missing accepted, rejected, and outcome values for replication, hosting, client performance, checksums, and maintenance decisions.

clusters.name: Git Object Representation Strategy
clusters.description: How Git objects are physically represented and transferred, distinguishing packfile-based layouts from distributed object-store alternatives.

relations.reading: Git Object Representation Strategy constrains Repository Storage Access Architecture
relations.rationale: Packfiles create random physical access patterns, making networked filesystems and whole-file caching unsuitable at very large repository counts.

values.label: Packfile-based object representation
values.description: Git objects are stored in packfiles, optionally using delta compression, rather than as separate loose objects.

values.label: Distributed key-value object storage
values.description: Maps Git objects directly into a distributed key-value store; rejected because DAG traversal requires costly sequential remote lookups.

values.label: DHT-backed object storage
values.description: Replaces on-disk packfiles with a distributed hash table; rejected because clone performance was unacceptable.

values.label: Distributed-store DAG round trips
values.description: Sequential remote fetches for DAG traversal create escalating latency and cost during ordinary Git operations.

values.label: Poor clone performance
values.description: Distributed object storage produced clone performance bad enough to invalidate the architecture.

values.label: Git-compatible native data format
values.description: Repositories remain ordinary Git data so standard Git tooling and client compatibility are preserved.

values.label: Packfiles in blob storage
values.description: Git packfiles are stored as scalable large-data blobs while operation state remains in the authoritative log.

values.label: Packfile- or Git-level distribution
values.description: Distribute repositories through packfile or Git-level mechanisms instead of filesystem distribution.

values.label: Filesystem dependence of packfiles
values.description: Packfiles require filesystem storage for Git access, creating server-side management pressure at scale.

values.label: Unsynchronized packfile fan-out
values.description: Packfiles are sent to all hosts without consensus synchronization because references keep them invisible until commit.

values.label: Synchronized packfile consensus
values.description: Large packfiles are synchronized through consensus before publication.

clusters.name: Repository Storage Access Path
clusters.description: How applications access repository data, including local, RPC-mediated, and networked storage paths.

relations.reading: Repository Storage Access Architecture affects Replica Consistency and Repair
relations.rationale: Remote repository access enables horizontal application scaling, while storage placement determines how replica availability and repair can be provided.

relations.reading: Repository Storage Access Architecture affects Replica Consistency and Repair
relations.rationale: Remote repository access enables horizontal application scaling, while storage placement determines how replica availability and repair can be provided.

relations.reading: Repository Storage Access Architecture affects Replica Consistency and Repair
relations.rationale: Remote repository access enables horizontal application scaling, while storage placement determines how replica availability and repair can be provided.

values.label: RPC-based repository access
values.description: Keeps repositories on dedicated fileservers while exposing repository operations remotely to applications.

values.label: Remote application repository operations
values.description: Moves Rails repository operations through the RPC layer instead of directly accessing distributed repository storage.

values.label: Networked filesystem storage
values.description: Uses file- or block-replicating networked filesystems for repositories; rejected because packfile random access performs poorly.

values.label: Block-level filesystem replication
values.description: Replicates repository storage at block level; rejected as operationally burdensome and insufficiently performant.

values.label: Whole-file packfile caching
values.description: Caches complete packfiles locally to improve random access; rejected because hundreds of thousands of repositories make it infeasible.

values.label: Single-machine repository placement
values.description: Leaves each repository on one fileserver, resulting in unresolved availability and hot-repository performance limitations.

values.label: Packfile-based protocol transfer
values.description: Git protocol transfers remain packfile-based regardless of server-side object storage, limiting alternative representations.

values.label: Faster geographically distributed transfers
values.description: Nearby synchronized replicas improve fetch and clone performance for geographically distant users.

values.label: Repository-location routing tables
values.description: Persistent tables tracking every repository's exact server location are avoided.

values.label: Native Git repositories on local NVMe storage
values.description: Complete ordinary repositories reside on local NVMe disks for random packfile reads and fast cloning.

values.label: Relational database for repository references
values.description: An external relational database tracks references to blob-stored packfiles.

values.label: Filesystem-level distribution of Git data
values.description: Distribute repository data through a filesystem while preserving the existing application interface.

values.label: Network-filesystem incompatibility with Git semantics
values.description: Git's local-filesystem assumptions create correctness and performance problems over networked filesystems.

values.label: Distributed-filesystem performance and correctness failure
values.description: Filesystem-distribution attempts remain slow and buggy at scale.

values.label: External repository-location routing table
values.description: An external database tracks every repository replica location across machines.

values.label: Single-repository HTTP daemon hosting
values.description: An HTTP daemon fronts one on-disk repository as a simple but low-scalability hosting arrangement.

values.label: Parallel repository operations
values.description: Distribution across disks and machines enables many Git operations to run concurrently.

clusters.name: Replica Write Ordering Strategy
clusters.description: How replicated reference writes select authority, order updates, and handle scheduling, consistency, and quorum constraints.

relations.reading: Replica Consistency and Repair Strategy affects Failure Detection and Request Routing
relations.rationale: Replica health and repair determine which repository copies request routing can safely use after server or network failures.

values.label: Majority-based write quorum
values.description: Accepts writes only after successful durable application on a replica majority.

values.label: Primaryless per-write voting
values.description: Uses a vote for each write to establish ordering and outcome instead of a permanently elected primary.

values.label: Single-primary write ordering
values.description: Uses one primary to establish write order for all replicas; explicitly rejected by Spokes.

values.label: Reference-update latency budget
values.description: Replica reference updates are required to complete within a few hundred milliseconds to sustain several updates per second.

values.label: Read-preserving write optimization
values.description: Reference-write scaling must improve write handling without slowing the much larger volume of reads.

values.label: Coalesced bookkeeping transactions
values.description: Many non-user reference updates are combined into fewer transactions to reduce cascade processing overhead.

values.label: Priority scheduling for user reference updates
values.description: User-initiated reference updates are scheduled ahead of non-time-critical bookkeeping work.

values.label: Bookkeeping-cascade processing delay
values.description: Large cascades of bookkeeping updates can keep a repository busy and delay or time out user requests.

values.label: Durability-gated write acceptance
values.description: Accept writes only when replication provides sufficient protection against permanent data loss.

values.label: Synchronous multi-replica write acceptance
values.description: Commit writes synchronously to at least two replicas before reporting success.

values.label: Consistency-and-partition-tolerant write policy
values.description: Prioritize consistency and partition tolerance over accepting writes without durable replication.

values.label: Unsafe write acceptance without durable commit
values.description: Accept writes even when they cannot yet be safely replicated.

values.label: Write unavailability under insufficient replication
values.description: Refuse writes temporarily when the minimum replica count cannot be achieved.

values.label: Arbitrary-server push acceptance
values.description: Any server may receive a repository push, with correctness independent of fixed primary ownership.

values.label: Eventually consistent repository replicas
values.description: Replicas may temporarily diverge after pushes or clones.

values.label: Replica-consistency complexity cost
values.description: Maintaining fully synchronized replicas imposes substantial implementation and operational complexity.

values.label: Slowest-replica latency bound
values.description: Consensus-step latency is bounded by the slowest participating replica.

values.label: Replica-count-driven push-throughput degradation
values.description: Increasing replica count raises coordination cost and reduces push throughput.

values.label: Horizontal scalability constraint of three-phase commit
values.description: Three-phase commit scales poorly because more replicas reduce performance while coordination remains mandatory.

values.label: Quorum-gated push acceptance
values.description: Pushes stop when a healthy authoritative quorum is unavailable.

values.label: Majority-exclusive write locking
values.description: Every write locks a replica majority exclusively to serialize updates and prevent conflicting concurrent writes.

values.label: Concurrent-write elimination
values.description: Majority locking eliminates concurrent writes and prevents divergent conflicting reference results.

clusters.name: Replica Commit Protocol
clusters.description: How repository reference transactions are validated, committed atomically, synchronized, and rolled back across replicas.

relations.reading: Replica Consistency and Repair Strategy affects Failure Detection and Request Routing
relations.rationale: Replica health and repair determine which repository copies request routing can safely use after server or network failures.

values.label: Non-majority write rollback
values.description: Reverts writes that failed to apply identically at a majority, preventing divergent replica state.

values.label: Three-phase replica commit
values.description: Reference-update transactions use three-phase commit to coordinate synchronization across replicas.

values.label: Transactional Git reference updates
values.description: Reference changes are exposed as transactions that replicas can validate, commit, or roll back together.

values.label: Deterministic replica transaction results
values.description: Transactions are designed to produce the same results on every replica.

values.label: Pre-acquired reference locks
values.description: All required local reference locks are acquired before transaction validation and commitment.

values.label: Reference-update precondition validation
values.description: Existing reference values and proposed new values are validated before commitment.

values.label: Atomic reference-update rollback
values.description: A failed validation rolls back the entire tentative reference transaction.

values.label: Reference-operation performance optimization
values.description: Reference operations are accelerated to reduce per-replica update time.

values.label: Atomic compare-and-swap WAL updates
values.description: Publish WAL index updates atomically using conditional update semantics.

values.label: Fully consistent replica synchronization
values.description: All replicated repository copies remain synchronized so pushes and clones immediately observe committed commits.

values.label: Single-local-copy reference synchronization
values.description: Synchronize reference transactions with one local repository copy rather than coordinating every replica.

clusters.name: Replica Repair and Redundancy Strategy
clusters.description: How replicas are kept available through dissent handling, reconstruction, repair, and replication factor.

relations.reading: Replica Consistency and Repair Strategy affects Failure Detection and Request Routing
relations.rationale: Replica health and repair determine which repository copies request routing can safely use after server or network failures.

values.label: Unhealthy dissenting replicas
values.description: Removes replicas that lose a write vote from read and write service until repaired.

values.label: Automatic replica repair
values.description: Restores unhealthy or missing replicas automatically while a healthy majority continues serving traffic.

values.label: N-to-N replica reconstruction
values.description: Rebuilds replicas anywhere in the cluster from any surviving replicas rather than from one designated source.

values.label: Three-way repository replication
values.description: Maintains three repository copies so an available, current replica remains routable after individual server failures.

values.label: Non-voting geo-replicated hosts
values.description: Geographically replicated hosts receive copies without participating in write votes, preserving push availability during their outages.

values.label: Durable highly available repository access
values.description: Multiple repository copies provide durable and highly available content access through server and network failures.

values.label: Reduced replication margin after server loss
values.description: A sudden server loss leaves repositories with fewer copies and no tolerance for another failure.

values.label: Higher write rejection risk after server loss
values.description: Reduced replication capacity increases the likelihood that subsequent writes are refused.

values.label: Excess idle-replica overhead for small repositories
values.description: A mandatory replica count leaves many lightly used repositories with mostly idle redundant capacity.

values.label: Insufficient replica capacity for massive monorepos
values.description: The fixed replica arrangement cannot provide enough capacity for traffic from very large repositories and CI.

values.label: Mandatory replica floor for every repository
values.description: Every repository retains at least three replicas to preserve consistency and redundancy.

values.label: Rendezvous-hashed repository placement
values.description: Repository placement is derived from repository identity and the current healthy-node set rather than persistent location records.

values.label: Elastic per-repository replica allocation
values.description: Adjust repository replica counts to demand rather than enforcing one fixed replication count.

values.label: Rack-level availability zones
values.description: Place repository replicas on separate racks to survive rack-wide failures.

values.label: Geographic disaster resilience
values.description: Disperse replicas across regions to survive broad geographic failures.

values.label: Distributed repository placement across disks and machines
values.description: Repository data is distributed across many disks and machines for parallelism and crash availability.

values.label: Repository availability during server crashes
values.description: Replicated repository data keeps repositories available when an individual hosting server fails.

values.label: Single-extra-copy redundancy
values.description: Relying on only one additional copy is insufficient for concurrent conflicting writes and stronger failure tolerance.

clusters.name: Failure Detection and Request Routing
clusters.description: How service failures are detected and how requests are redirected while avoiding false removal of healthy servers.

relations.reading: Failure Detection and Request Routing affects Planned Maintenance Continuity
relations.rationale: Failure classification and routing behavior determine whether maintenance can drain traffic without interrupting active operations.

values.label: Real-traffic failure detection
values.description: Uses failures encountered during real authenticated Git operations to test application, disk, and execution paths.

values.label: Heartbeat-only failure detection
values.description: Uses heartbeats as the sole detector; rejected because they react slowly and exercise limited functionality.

values.label: Three-consecutive-failure threshold
values.description: Marks a node offline only after three consecutive request failures, filtering ordinary application-level errors.

values.label: False offline marking
values.description: The threshold can occasionally remove a healthy node after coincidental consecutive failures.

values.label: Secondary heartbeat monitoring
values.description: Use heartbeats for load polling and recovery confirmation while operation failures remain primary.

values.label: Ordered multi-replica request routing
values.description: Return current replicas in preference order so requests can use the next available copy.

values.label: Replica failover on clean failures
values.description: Retry an operation on another repository replica after refusal or timeout.

values.label: Per-application-server failure views
values.description: Maintain failure state separately at each application server to represent asymmetric observations.

values.label: Cross-server fault-source inference
values.description: Compare failure reports to distinguish file-server faults from application-server or network faults.

values.label: Failure-aware request routing
values.description: Detects degraded servers and routes requests to available repository replicas.

values.label: Geo-replica read routing
values.description: Fetches and clones are directed to the closest replica that is sufficiently synchronized.

values.label: Nearest-replica Git reads
values.description: Route Git reads to the geographically nearest repository replica.

clusters.name: Planned Maintenance Continuity
clusters.description: How planned server reboots and retirement preserve active work, replica currency, and availability during controlled transitions.

relations.reading: Planned Maintenance Continuity requires Replica Consistency and Repair Strategy to be decided first
relations.rationale: Quiescing and continued write delivery depend on replicated copies and the system’s ability to keep a maintenance target synchronized.

relations.reading: Planned Maintenance Continuity requires Replica Consistency and Repair Strategy to be decided first
relations.rationale: Quiescing and continued write delivery depend on replicated copies and the system’s ability to keep a maintenance target synchronized.

relations.reading: Planned Maintenance Continuity requires Replica Consistency and Repair Strategy to be decided first
relations.rationale: Quiescing and continued write delivery depend on replicated copies and the system’s ability to keep a maintenance target synchronized.

values.label: Failure-mechanism reuse for maintenance
values.description: Applies crash and permanent-failure handling mechanisms to planned reboots and server retirement.

values.label: Quiescing before reboot
values.description: Stops new reads while allowing active operations to complete before a server reboots.

values.label: Continued write delivery during quiescing
values.description: Continues sending writes to the quiescing replica so it does not fall arbitrarily behind.

values.label: Immediate reboot
values.description: Reboots without draining activity; rejected because it can interrupt long-running reads and clones.

values.label: Lost interrupted-clone progress
values.description: An interrupted large clone must restart elsewhere and loses progress already completed.

values.label: Replica catch-up load
values.description: Withheld writes would make a quiescing replica fall behind and create substantial recovery work.

values.label: Planned rolling reboot operations
values.description: Use sequential, bounded rolling reboots to test or perform changes while preserving service continuity.

values.label: Unplanned server reboot testing
values.description: Use random abrupt reboots as the primary test of single-node failure handling.

values.label: Unplanned server unplugging for retirement
values.description: Retire servers by abruptly unplugging them without quiescing active work.

clusters.name: Client Repository Materialization Strategy
clusters.description: How clients obtain and populate large repositories, including virtualized, sparse, and demand-fetched working data.

relations.reading: Client Large-Repository Performance Strategy affects Packfile Lifecycle Management
relations.rationale: Client performance depends partly on pack counts, file-handle pressure, delta layout, and background maintenance efficiency.

relations.reading: Client Large-Repository Performance Strategy requires Git Object Representation Strategy to be decided first
relations.rationale: Virtualized cloning and client optimizations must accommodate the Git object and packfile representation used by the hosting protocol.

values.label: Virtualized filesystem
values.description: Uses a virtualized filesystem to hide most of a very large repository from the client working environment.

values.label: Non-virtualized large-repository support
values.description: Improves Git so very large repositories can be supported without requiring filesystem virtualization.

values.label: GVFS-protocol cloning
values.description: Retains virtualization-based cloning through Azure Repos for especially large hosted repositories.

values.label: Central-server missing-object dependency
values.description: Clients rely on a central server for objects absent from the initial materialization.

values.label: Commit-and-tree-only initial clone
values.description: Initial clones transfer commits and trees while omitting other object classes.

values.label: On-demand object downloading
values.description: Objects are fetched when checkout or another client operation requires them.

values.label: Sparse-checkout demand-fetch integration
values.description: Sparse working trees reduce the objects required through integrated demand fetching.

values.label: Co-located object cache servers
values.description: Nearby cache servers proxy object transfers to reduce latency, central load, and bandwidth pressure.

values.label: Complete object transfer burden
values.description: Traditional cloning transfers all referenced history and objects, imposing substantial network and server cost.

values.label: Client-side object verification burden
values.description: Hash verification for the very large transferred object set imposes substantial client processing cost.

values.label: No cache server for undersized GVFS repositories
values.description: Use GVFS without a co-located cache server when repository and user scale do not justify cache infrastructure.

values.label: Git protocol with Scalar registration
values.description: Use the Git protocol with Scalar registration when GVFS cache infrastructure is unavailable or unjustified.

values.label: GVFS under insufficient cache infrastructure
values.description: Adopt GVFS despite lacking the resources needed to operate its cache-server infrastructure.

values.label: Sparse working-directory default
values.description: Client cloning initially populates only a small selected portion of the repository working directory.

values.label: Full working-directory materialization
values.description: Clients may explicitly override sparse mode and populate the complete working directory.

values.label: Populated-file minimization priority
values.description: Materialization minimizes populated files because file data movement and modification detection dominate operational cost.

values.label: Populated-file data-transfer cost
values.description: Populating files requires substantially more data movement than changing index entries.

values.label: Populated-file modification-detection cost
values.description: Detecting user modifications becomes especially expensive as the number of populated files grows.

values.label: Nested source working-directory layout
values.description: The repository directory contains a focused source working directory with room for sibling non-Git build outputs.

values.label: Sibling build-output directories
values.description: Build artifacts reside outside the Git-managed working directory to reduce repository-management workload.

values.label: Reduced Git working-directory workload
values.description: Sparse population and separated build outputs reduce the work Git performs over client files.

values.label: GVFS protocol as standard Git feature
values.description: The GVFS-specific protocol is treated as a service-specific predecessor rather than a standard Git feature.

values.label: Virtualized filesystem for populated-size scaling
values.description: A virtualized filesystem defers populated working-tree costs and accelerates checkout.

values.label: Full local copy of reachable objects
values.description: Clients store every reachable repository object locally rather than retrieving missing objects on demand.

clusters.name: Client Git Performance Mechanisms
clusters.description: Which Git-native optimizations, tracing, and command mechanisms improve large-repository client performance.

relations.reading: Client Large-Repository Performance Strategy affects Packfile Lifecycle Management
relations.rationale: Client performance depends partly on pack counts, file-handle pressure, delta layout, and background maintenance efficiency.

relations.reading: Client Large-Repository Performance Strategy requires Git Object Representation Strategy to be decided first
relations.rationale: Virtualized cloning and client optimizations must accommodate the Git object and packfile representation used by the hosting protocol.

values.label: Custom performance tracing and feedback
values.description: Uses tracing and user feedback to locate client bottlenecks in large-repository workflows.

values.label: Commit-graph optimization
values.description: Uses commit-graph files to improve large-repository Git performance.

values.label: Push and sparse-checkout optimization
values.description: Improves push and sparse-checkout behavior for large repositories.

values.label: Core Git performance investment
values.description: Moves required performance capabilities into Git itself to reduce dependence on management layers.

values.label: Filesystem change monitoring
values.description: Git uses filesystem event monitoring to identify changed paths instead of scanning every populated path.

values.label: Modified-path-focused index inspection
values.description: Index inspection is limited to paths identified as modified.

values.label: Reduced git-status latency
values.description: Filesystem monitoring and focused inspection substantially reduce status latency in large sparse repositories.

values.label: Background split reachable commit-graph maintenance
values.description: Update reachable commit graphs incrementally in the background to reduce foreground fetch overhead.

values.label: Foreground fetch commit-graph overhead
values.description: Writing commit-graph data during foreground fetch increases user-visible fetch work.

values.label: Core-command working-directory inspection
values.description: Core Git commands inspect working-directory state against the index and on-disk files.

values.label: Complete tracked-path index
values.description: The index represents every tracked path at HEAD and is read and written by core commands.

values.label: Updated compressed index format
values.description: A revised index representation compresses very large indexes and reduces single-file read/write burden.

values.label: Untracked cache feature
values.description: Git's untracked cache reduces repeated filesystem work in repositories with many files.

values.label: Index-size reduction
values.description: The revised index reduces the reported index size from 400 MB to 250 MB.

values.label: Low per-entry index processing time
values.description: Per-entry processing remains low because the principal cost is streaming one index file for reading and writing.

values.label: Ahead-behind status calculation disablement
values.description: Disable ahead-behind comparison when status primarily needs unstaged-change information.

values.label: Watchman filesystem watcher
values.description: A general-purpose Watchman watcher is used for Git working-tree change detection.

clusters.name: Client Repository Management Strategy
clusters.description: How a management layer configures, maintains, scopes, and transitions large-repository client support.

relations.reading: Client Large-Repository Performance Strategy affects Packfile Lifecycle Management
relations.rationale: Client performance depends partly on pack counts, file-handle pressure, delta layout, and background maintenance efficiency.

relations.rationale: Virtualized cloning and client optimizations must accommodate the Git object and packfile representation used by the hosting protocol.

values.label: Scalar configuration and maintenance
values.description: Uses Scalar to apply recommended configuration and run background maintenance that accelerates Git workflows.

values.label: Reduced Scalar scope
values.description: Limits Scalar to currently needed performance capabilities rather than expanding its management role.

values.label: Transitional Scalar layer
values.description: Uses Scalar temporarily while Git develops capabilities that can eventually replace it.

values.label: Git-native Scalar replacement
values.description: Contributes Scalar-driven management features to Git so external layers can be removed over time.

values.label: User-controlled maintenance suspension
values.description: Users can pause or unregister background repository maintenance.

values.label: Repository-local maintenance logging
values.description: Maintenance activity and durations are recorded in the repository for user visibility.

values.label: Scalar repository registration
values.description: Repositories are explicitly activated with Scalar before it applies repository-specific configuration and maintenance.

values.label: Repository-local Git configuration
values.description: Scalar stores client behavior settings in the repository's local Git configuration.

values.label: Background scheduled fetching
values.description: Fetch remote objects periodically in the background while keeping user-visible remote references unchanged.

values.label: Hidden remote-reference namespace
values.description: Store background-fetch references outside the visible remote-reference namespace for maintenance use.

values.label: Foreground-only remote-reference updates
values.description: Require foreground fetches when users need visible remote-reference updates.

values.label: Background repository configuration updates
values.description: Apply recommended repository configuration changes asynchronously after installation.

values.label: Custom Git distribution for Scalar
values.description: Scalar is shipped within a custom Git distribution while broader fork compatibility is pursued.

values.label: Compatibility-driven default-off optimization features
values.description: Advanced performance features remain disabled by default to preserve broad compatibility.

clusters.name: Packfile Lifecycle Management
clusters.description: How packfiles are consolidated, indexed, redirected, and deleted without exhausting file handles or disrupting foreground Git operations.

values.label: Incremental small-batch repacking
values.description: Rewrites bounded batches of small packfiles instead of attempting unlimited or repository-wide repacking.

values.label: Multi-pack-index object relocation
values.description: Uses the multi-pack-index to redirect objects into newly created packs while avoiding reads from superseded packs.

values.label: Two-phase consolidation and expiration
values.description: Separates pack creation and reference updates from deletion so cleanup occurs only after old packs are unreferenced.

values.label: Deferred unreferenced-pack deletion
values.description: Retains old packs until their objects have been redirected and no references remain.

values.label: Foreground-command continuity
values.description: Designs maintenance so foreground Git commands continue operating during repacking and expiration.

values.label: Unbounded packfile growth
values.description: Allows pack counts to grow without bound, creating file-handle scalability problems.

values.label: Pack-count and storage reduction
values.description: Deployment reduced repositories from thousands of packs and 150–200 GB to fewer than 100 packs and 30–50 GB.

values.label: Loose-object cleanup
values.description: Maintenance removes accumulated loose objects to reduce storage and lookup overhead.

values.label: Single-pack full repacking
values.description: All repository data is rewritten into one packfile to reduce lookup overhead.

values.label: Pack-index accumulation lookup cost
values.description: Accumulating packfiles increases the number of indexes Git must inspect and slows object lookup.

values.label: Background incremental repository maintenance
values.description: Perform repository cleanup and rewriting incrementally in background processes rather than blocking foreground commands.

values.label: Foreground automatic garbage collection
values.description: Run complete automatic garbage collection synchronously at the end of user commands.

values.label: Foreground garbage-collection blocking
values.description: Foreground garbage collection blocks commands and can exhaust CPU and memory during repository rewrites.

values.label: Performance decay from disabled automatic collection
values.description: Avoid foreground collection but allow accumulated objects to gradually degrade Git performance.

values.label: Primary-only compaction scheduling
values.description: Schedule repository compaction on only the primary replica and propagate its results to peers.

values.label: WAL-propagated compaction events
values.description: Propagate compaction results through the WAL so replicas apply the same repository maintenance events.

values.label: S3 distribution of compacted packs
values.description: Distribute already-compacted packs from object storage instead of repacking independently on replicas.

values.label: Periodic write-ahead-log compaction
values.description: Compact the WAL periodically to bound restoration work as updates accumulate.

values.label: On-disk layout optimization for compaction
values.description: Optimize repository disk layout to reduce compaction impact on ingestion.

values.label: Compaction-limited push throughput
values.description: Push throughput becomes bounded by on-disk compaction speed after WAL latency is reduced.

values.label: Replica-local repository repacking
values.description: Repack repositories independently on each replica.

values.label: Replica failover from concurrent maintenance
values.description: Concurrent compaction on replicas can trigger repository failover and reduce availability.

values.label: Automatic Git garbage-collection disablement
values.description: Disable foreground automatic garbage collection and shift cleanup to background maintenance.

clusters.name: Repository Replication Layer
clusters.description: Which system layer and mechanism performs repository replication across hosts.

relations.reading: Repository Replication Layer affects Replica Write Coordination Strategy
relations.rationale: The new documents state that geographic replica distance adds latency and constrains reference-update throughput.

relations.reading: Repository Replication Layer affects Replica Write Coordination Strategy
relations.rationale: The new documents state that geographic replica distance adds latency and constrains reference-update throughput.

values.label: DRBD block-level replication
values.description: Replication is performed below the application at the filesystem block level.

values.label: Co-located replica placement
values.description: Replicas are kept physically close to satisfy block-replication latency constraints.

values.label: Application-level Spokes replication
values.description: An application-level system replicates Git repositories and manages their copies across file servers.

values.label: Distant replica placement
values.description: Replicas are deliberately distributed across greater geographic distances despite added latency.

values.label: Git-and-rsync replication
values.description: Replication combines Git-aware operations with rsync for copying, repair, and rebalancing.

values.label: S3-backed write-ahead-log authority
values.description: Authoritative repository state is retained in durable object storage while hosts serve reconstructible working copies.

values.label: WAL-based repository provenance and replica rewind
values.description: The authoritative log records repository operations so states can be reconstructed, rewound, and fast-forwarded.

values.label: Optimistic UDP gossip replication
values.description: Exchange replica catch-up metadata through lossy gossip while retaining authoritative recovery from the WAL.

values.label: ETag-validated replica freshness
values.description: Validate replica currency against the WAL index before serving reads.

values.label: WAL-index catch-up before reads
values.description: Catch replicas up from a newer WAL index before serving fetches or clones.

values.label: S3-backed globally consistent reads
values.description: Use authoritative S3 state checks so replicas expose a consistent repository view despite message loss or topology changes.

values.label: Arbitrary replica-count scaling
values.description: Scale read-serving capacity by deploying an arbitrary number of consistent replicas.

values.label: Fully consistent replica cluster
values.description: Maintain full consistency across replicas while adding read and RPC serving capacity.

values.label: WAL-first storage design
values.description: Use the write-ahead log as the primary durability and replication foundation for repository updates.

values.label: S3 Express One Zone WAL storage
values.description: Use low-latency S3 Express One Zone as the WAL persistence layer for high push rates.

values.label: Batched WAL operations
values.description: Batch WAL writes to reduce object-store latency and sustain high push ingestion rates.

values.label: Low-latency replica placement
values.description: Place replicas close enough to sustain high-rate update coordination.

values.label: Single-S3-write-per-push model
values.description: Persist each push with one object-store write.

values.label: On-disk repository consensus authority
values.description: Repository copies on disk serve as the authoritative state for consensus and correctness.

values.label: Individually managed repository copies
values.description: Each repository copy is treated as a valuable, individually tracked operational asset.

values.label: Continuous repository checksum tracking
values.description: Replica checksums are continuously maintained to detect corruption in authoritative repository copies.

values.label: Repository-operation burden at scale
values.description: Per-repository tracking, verification, corruption detection, and urgent repair create operational burden as scale grows.

values.label: Per-update replica checksum validation
values.description: Replica logical contents are checked after each update using a checksum over reference-value state.

values.label: Incremental checksum maintenance
values.description: Replica checksums are updated incrementally instead of recomputed from scratch after every reference update.

values.label: XOR-based checksum updates
values.description: Reference changes update replica checksums by XORing out old pairs and XORing in new pairs.

values.label: From-scratch checksum recomputation
values.description: The checksum is fully recomputed for every update, imposing excessive cost in busy repositories.

clusters.name: Repository Hosting Model
clusters.description: Which collaboration and hosting model combines client decentralization with repository service centralization?

values.label: Distributed version-control model
values.description: Clients retain decentralized version-control capabilities while collaborating through hosted repositories.

values.label: Centralized repository hosting
values.description: Organizations rely on a central host for shared repository collaboration despite distributed client capabilities.

values.label: Hybrid distributed-client centralized-host architecture
values.description: Distributed client workflows such as offline work and delayed pushes operate against centralized repository hosting.

values.label: Git repository hosting difficulty
values.description: Hosting Git repositories creates substantial scalability and operational complexity.

values.label: Distributed Git implementation
values.description: The hosting system itself distributes or modifies Git rather than retaining standard Git as the implementation boundary.

clusters.name: Repository Cache Materialization Strategy
clusters.description: How repository state is cached, discarded, and reconstructed to balance local responsiveness, storage cost, and materialization work.

values.label: Local-disk repository warm cache
values.description: Hosts keep repositories as local working copies for efficient access without making local placement authoritative.

values.label: On-demand repository materialization
values.description: A missing repository is reconstructed from authoritative log state on the host that needs to serve it.

values.label: Idle-replica disk garbage collection
values.description: Remove inactive repository replicas from local disk to reduce retained storage.

values.label: On-demand replica rematerialization
values.description: Reconstruct an evicted repository replica from the WAL when demand returns.

clusters.name: Git Object Storage Format
clusters.description: Which physical format stores Git objects, including packfiles and distributed object-store representations.

relations.reading: Git Object Representation Strategy constrains Repository Storage Access Architecture
relations.rationale: Packfiles create random physical access patterns, making networked filesystems and whole-file caching unsuitable at very large repository counts.

relations.reading: Git Object Representation Strategy constrains Repository Storage Access Architecture
relations.rationale: Packfiles create random physical access patterns, making networked filesystems and whole-file caching unsuitable at very large repository counts.

values.label: Packfile-based object representation
values.description: Git objects are stored in packfiles, optionally using delta compression, rather than as separate loose objects.

values.label: Distributed key-value object storage
values.description: Maps Git objects directly into a distributed key-value store; rejected because DAG traversal requires costly sequential remote lookups.

values.label: DHT-backed object storage
values.description: Replaces on-disk packfiles with a distributed hash table; rejected because clone performance was unacceptable.

values.label: Git-compatible native data format
values.description: Repositories remain ordinary Git data so standard Git tooling and client compatibility are preserved.

values.label: Packfiles in blob storage
values.description: Git packfiles are stored as scalable large-data blobs while operation state remains in the authoritative log.

clusters.name: Git Object Distribution Consistency
clusters.description: How Git object data is distributed and synchronized across storage locations, including packfile fan-out and consensus.

relations.reading: Git Object Representation Strategy constrains Repository Storage Access Architecture
relations.rationale: Packfiles create random physical access patterns, making networked filesystems and whole-file caching unsuitable at very large repository counts.

relations.reading: Git Object Representation Strategy constrains Repository Storage Access Architecture
relations.rationale: Packfiles create random physical access patterns, making networked filesystems and whole-file caching unsuitable at very large repository counts.

values.label: Distributed-store DAG round trips
values.description: Sequential remote fetches for DAG traversal create escalating latency and cost during ordinary Git operations.

values.label: Poor clone performance
values.description: Distributed object storage produced clone performance bad enough to invalidate the architecture.

values.label: Packfile- or Git-level distribution
values.description: Distribute repositories through packfile or Git-level mechanisms instead of filesystem distribution.

values.label: Filesystem dependence of packfiles
values.description: Packfiles require filesystem storage for Git access, creating server-side management pressure at scale.

values.label: Unsynchronized packfile fan-out
values.description: Packfiles are sent to all hosts without consensus synchronization because references keep them invisible until commit.

values.label: Synchronized packfile consensus
values.description: Large packfiles are synchronized through consensus before publication.

clusters.name: Repository Access Mechanism
clusters.description: Which local, remote, filesystem, RPC, or protocol mechanism applications use to perform repository operations.

relations.reading: Repository Storage Access Architecture affects Replica Consistency and Repair
relations.rationale: Remote repository access enables horizontal application scaling, while storage placement determines how replica availability and repair can be provided.

relations.reading: Repository Storage Access Architecture affects Replica Consistency and Repair
relations.rationale: Remote repository access enables horizontal application scaling, while storage placement determines how replica availability and repair can be provided.

relations.reading: Repository Storage Access Architecture affects Replica Consistency and Repair
relations.rationale: Remote repository access enables horizontal application scaling, while storage placement determines how replica availability and repair can be provided.

relations.reading: Repository Storage Access Architecture affects Replica Consistency and Repair
relations.rationale: Remote repository access enables horizontal application scaling, while storage placement determines how replica availability and repair can be provided.

values.label: RPC-based repository access
values.description: Keeps repositories on dedicated fileservers while exposing repository operations remotely to applications.

values.label: Remote application repository operations
values.description: Moves Rails repository operations through the RPC layer instead of directly accessing distributed repository storage.

values.label: Networked filesystem storage
values.description: Uses file- or block-replicating networked filesystems for repositories; rejected because packfile random access performs poorly.

values.label: Block-level filesystem replication
values.description: Replicates repository storage at block level; rejected as operationally burdensome and insufficiently performant.

values.label: Whole-file packfile caching
values.description: Caches complete packfiles locally to improve random access; rejected because hundreds of thousands of repositories make it infeasible.

values.label: Packfile-based protocol transfer
values.description: Git protocol transfers remain packfile-based regardless of server-side object storage, limiting alternative representations.

values.label: Native Git repositories on local NVMe storage
values.description: Complete ordinary repositories reside on local NVMe disks for random packfile reads and fast cloning.

values.label: Filesystem-level distribution of Git data
values.description: Distribute repository data through a filesystem while preserving the existing application interface.

values.label: Network-filesystem incompatibility with Git semantics
values.description: Git's local-filesystem assumptions create correctness and performance problems over networked filesystems.

values.label: Distributed-filesystem performance and correctness failure
values.description: Filesystem-distribution attempts remain slow and buggy at scale.

values.label: Single-repository HTTP daemon hosting
values.description: An HTTP daemon fronts one on-disk repository as a simple but low-scalability hosting arrangement.

values.label: Parallel repository operations
values.description: Distribution across disks and machines enables many Git operations to run concurrently.

values.label: Relational database for repository references
values.description: An external relational database tracks references to blob-stored packfiles.

clusters.name: Repository Placement and Routing
clusters.description: How repositories are physically placed and how their locations or transfers are selected across machines and sites.

relations.reading: Repository Storage Access Architecture affects Replica Consistency and Repair
relations.rationale: Remote repository access enables horizontal application scaling, while storage placement determines how replica availability and repair can be provided.

relations.reading: Repository Storage Access Architecture affects Replica Consistency and Repair
relations.rationale: Remote repository access enables horizontal application scaling, while storage placement determines how replica availability and repair can be provided.

relations.reading: Repository Storage Access Architecture affects Replica Consistency and Repair
relations.rationale: Remote repository access enables horizontal application scaling, while storage placement determines how replica availability and repair can be provided.

relations.reading: Repository Storage Access Architecture affects Replica Consistency and Repair
relations.rationale: Remote repository access enables horizontal application scaling, while storage placement determines how replica availability and repair can be provided.

values.label: Single-machine repository placement
values.description: Leaves each repository on one fileserver, resulting in unresolved availability and hot-repository performance limitations.

values.label: Faster geographically distributed transfers
values.description: Nearby synchronized replicas improve fetch and clone performance for geographically distant users.

values.label: Repository-location routing tables
values.description: Persistent tables tracking every repository's exact server location are avoided.

values.label: External repository-location routing table
values.description: An external database tracks every repository replica location across machines.

clusters.name: Replica Write Authority and Quorum
clusters.description: Which replicas may accept reference writes and what durability, consistency, quorum, and authority rules govern acceptance.

relations.reading: Replica Consistency and Repair Strategy affects Failure Detection and Request Routing
relations.rationale: Replica health and repair determine which repository copies request routing can safely use after server or network failures.

relations.reading: Replica Consistency and Repair Strategy affects Failure Detection and Request Routing
relations.rationale: Replica health and repair determine which repository copies request routing can safely use after server or network failures.

values.label: Majority-based write quorum
values.description: Accepts writes only after successful durable application on a replica majority.

values.label: Primaryless per-write voting
values.description: Uses a vote for each write to establish ordering and outcome instead of a permanently elected primary.

values.label: Single-primary write ordering
values.description: Uses one primary to establish write order for all replicas; explicitly rejected by Spokes.

values.label: Durability-gated write acceptance
values.description: Accept writes only when replication provides sufficient protection against permanent data loss.

values.label: Synchronous multi-replica write acceptance
values.description: Commit writes synchronously to at least two replicas before reporting success.

values.label: Consistency-and-partition-tolerant write policy
values.description: Prioritize consistency and partition tolerance over accepting writes without durable replication.

values.label: Unsafe write acceptance without durable commit
values.description: Accept writes even when they cannot yet be safely replicated.

values.label: Write unavailability under insufficient replication
values.description: Refuse writes temporarily when the minimum replica count cannot be achieved.

values.label: Arbitrary-server push acceptance
values.description: Any server may receive a repository push, with correctness independent of fixed primary ownership.

values.label: Eventually consistent repository replicas
values.description: Replicas may temporarily diverge after pushes or clones.

values.label: Quorum-gated push acceptance
values.description: Pushes stop when a healthy authoritative quorum is unavailable.

clusters.name: Reference Write Scheduling
clusters.description: How replicated reference writes are prioritized, coalesced, delayed, and bounded for latency and throughput.

relations.reading: Replica Consistency and Repair Strategy affects Failure Detection and Request Routing
relations.rationale: Replica health and repair determine which repository copies request routing can safely use after server or network failures.

relations.reading: Replica Consistency and Repair Strategy affects Failure Detection and Request Routing
relations.rationale: Replica health and repair determine which repository copies request routing can safely use after server or network failures.

values.label: Reference-update latency budget
values.description: Replica reference updates are required to complete within a few hundred milliseconds to sustain several updates per second.

values.label: Read-preserving write optimization
values.description: Reference-write scaling must improve write handling without slowing the much larger volume of reads.

values.label: Coalesced bookkeeping transactions
values.description: Many non-user reference updates are combined into fewer transactions to reduce cascade processing overhead.

values.label: Priority scheduling for user reference updates
values.description: User-initiated reference updates are scheduled ahead of non-time-critical bookkeeping work.

values.label: Bookkeeping-cascade processing delay
values.description: Large cascades of bookkeeping updates can keep a repository busy and delay or time out user requests.

values.label: Replica-consistency complexity cost
values.description: Maintaining fully synchronized replicas imposes substantial implementation and operational complexity.

values.label: Slowest-replica latency bound
values.description: Consensus-step latency is bounded by the slowest participating replica.

values.label: Replica-count-driven push-throughput degradation
values.description: Increasing replica count raises coordination cost and reduces push throughput.

values.label: Horizontal scalability constraint of three-phase commit
values.description: Three-phase commit scales poorly because more replicas reduce performance while coordination remains mandatory.

clusters.name: Replica Commit Protocol
clusters.description: How repository reference transactions are validated, committed atomically, synchronized, and rolled back across replicas.

relations.reading: Replica Consistency and Repair Strategy affects Failure Detection and Request Routing
relations.rationale: Replica health and repair determine which repository copies request routing can safely use after server or network failures.

relations.reading: Replica Consistency and Repair Strategy affects Failure Detection and Request Routing
relations.rationale: Replica health and repair determine which repository copies request routing can safely use after server or network failures.

values.label: Non-majority write rollback
values.description: Reverts writes that failed to apply identically at a majority, preventing divergent replica state.

values.label: Three-phase replica commit
values.description: Reference-update transactions use three-phase commit to coordinate synchronization across replicas.

values.label: Transactional Git reference updates
values.description: Reference changes are exposed as transactions that replicas can validate, commit, or roll back together.

values.label: Deterministic replica transaction results
values.description: Transactions are designed to produce the same results on every replica.

values.label: Pre-acquired reference locks
values.description: All required local reference locks are acquired before transaction validation and commitment.

values.label: Reference-update precondition validation
values.description: Existing reference values and proposed new values are validated before commitment.

values.label: Atomic reference-update rollback
values.description: A failed validation rolls back the entire tentative reference transaction.

values.label: Reference-operation performance optimization
values.description: Reference operations are accelerated to reduce per-replica update time.

values.label: Atomic compare-and-swap WAL updates
values.description: Publish WAL index updates atomically using conditional update semantics.

values.label: Fully consistent replica synchronization
values.description: All replicated repository copies remain synchronized so pushes and clones immediately observe committed commits.

values.label: Single-local-copy reference synchronization
values.description: Synchronize reference transactions with one local repository copy rather than coordinating every replica.

values.label: Majority-exclusive write locking
values.description: Every write locks a replica majority exclusively to serialize updates and prevent conflicting concurrent writes.

values.label: Concurrent-write elimination
values.description: Majority locking eliminates concurrent writes and prevents divergent conflicting reference results.

clusters.name: Replica Repair and Redundancy Strategy
clusters.description: How replicas are kept available through dissent handling, reconstruction, repair, and replication factor.

relations.reading: Replica Consistency and Repair Strategy affects Failure Detection and Request Routing
relations.rationale: Replica health and repair determine which repository copies request routing can safely use after server or network failures.

relations.reading: Replica Consistency and Repair Strategy affects Failure Detection and Request Routing
relations.rationale: Replica health and repair determine which repository copies request routing can safely use after server or network failures.

values.label: Unhealthy dissenting replicas
values.description: Removes replicas that lose a write vote from read and write service until repaired.

values.label: Automatic replica repair
values.description: Restores unhealthy or missing replicas automatically while a healthy majority continues serving traffic.

values.label: N-to-N replica reconstruction
values.description: Rebuilds replicas anywhere in the cluster from any surviving replicas rather than from one designated source.

values.label: Three-way repository replication
values.description: Maintains three repository copies so an available, current replica remains routable after individual server failures.

values.label: Non-voting geo-replicated hosts
values.description: Geographically replicated hosts receive copies without participating in write votes, preserving push availability during their outages.

values.label: Durable highly available repository access
values.description: Multiple repository copies provide durable and highly available content access through server and network failures.

values.label: Reduced replication margin after server loss
values.description: A sudden server loss leaves repositories with fewer copies and no tolerance for another failure.

values.label: Higher write rejection risk after server loss
values.description: Reduced replication capacity increases the likelihood that subsequent writes are refused.

values.label: Excess idle-replica overhead for small repositories
values.description: A mandatory replica count leaves many lightly used repositories with mostly idle redundant capacity.

values.label: Insufficient replica capacity for massive monorepos
values.description: The fixed replica arrangement cannot provide enough capacity for traffic from very large repositories and CI.

values.label: Mandatory replica floor for every repository
values.description: Every repository retains at least three replicas to preserve consistency and redundancy.

values.label: Rendezvous-hashed repository placement
values.description: Repository placement is derived from repository identity and the current healthy-node set rather than persistent location records.

values.label: Elastic per-repository replica allocation
values.description: Adjust repository replica counts to demand rather than enforcing one fixed replication count.

values.label: Rack-level availability zones
values.description: Place repository replicas on separate racks to survive rack-wide failures.

values.label: Geographic disaster resilience
values.description: Disperse replicas across regions to survive broad geographic failures.

values.label: Distributed repository placement across disks and machines
values.description: Repository data is distributed across many disks and machines for parallelism and crash availability.

values.label: Repository availability during server crashes
values.description: Replicated repository data keeps repositories available when an individual hosting server fails.

values.label: Single-extra-copy redundancy
values.description: Relying on only one additional copy is insufficient for concurrent conflicting writes and stronger failure tolerance.

clusters.name: Failure Detection Strategy
clusters.description: Which signals and thresholds determine whether a repository server is considered failed or offline.

relations.reading: Failure Detection and Request Routing affects Planned Maintenance Continuity
relations.rationale: Failure classification and routing behavior determine whether maintenance can drain traffic without interrupting active operations.

values.label: Real-traffic failure detection
values.description: Uses failures encountered during real authenticated Git operations to test application, disk, and execution paths.

values.label: Heartbeat-only failure detection
values.description: Uses heartbeats as the sole detector; rejected because they react slowly and exercise limited functionality.

values.label: Three-consecutive-failure threshold
values.description: Marks a node offline only after three consecutive request failures, filtering ordinary application-level errors.

values.label: False offline marking
values.description: The threshold can occasionally remove a healthy node after coincidental consecutive failures.

values.label: Secondary heartbeat monitoring
values.description: Use heartbeats for load polling and recovery confirmation while operation failures remain primary.

clusters.name: Replica Request Routing
clusters.description: How requests are directed among replicas after considering server health, ordering, geography, and failover.

relations.reading: Failure Detection and Request Routing affects Planned Maintenance Continuity
relations.rationale: Failure classification and routing behavior determine whether maintenance can drain traffic without interrupting active operations.

values.label: Ordered multi-replica request routing
values.description: Return current replicas in preference order so requests can use the next available copy.

values.label: Replica failover on clean failures
values.description: Retry an operation on another repository replica after refusal or timeout.

values.label: Per-application-server failure views
values.description: Maintain failure state separately at each application server to represent asymmetric observations.

values.label: Cross-server fault-source inference
values.description: Compare failure reports to distinguish file-server faults from application-server or network faults.

values.label: Failure-aware request routing
values.description: Detects degraded servers and routes requests to available repository replicas.

values.label: Geo-replica read routing
values.description: Fetches and clones are directed to the closest replica that is sufficiently synchronized.

values.label: Nearest-replica Git reads
values.description: Route Git reads to the geographically nearest repository replica.

clusters.name: Planned Maintenance Continuity
clusters.description: How planned server reboots and retirement preserve active work, replica currency, and availability during controlled transitions.

relations.reading: Planned Maintenance Continuity requires Replica Consistency and Repair Strategy to be decided first
relations.rationale: Quiescing and continued write delivery depend on replicated copies and the system’s ability to keep a maintenance target synchronized.

relations.reading: Planned Maintenance Continuity requires Replica Consistency and Repair Strategy to be decided first
relations.rationale: Quiescing and continued write delivery depend on replicated copies and the system’s ability to keep a maintenance target synchronized.

relations.reading: Planned Maintenance Continuity requires Replica Consistency and Repair Strategy to be decided first
relations.rationale: Quiescing and continued write delivery depend on replicated copies and the system’s ability to keep a maintenance target synchronized.

relations.reading: Planned Maintenance Continuity requires Replica Consistency and Repair Strategy to be decided first
relations.rationale: Quiescing and continued write delivery depend on replicated copies and the system’s ability to keep a maintenance target synchronized.

values.label: Failure-mechanism reuse for maintenance
values.description: Applies crash and permanent-failure handling mechanisms to planned reboots and server retirement.

values.label: Quiescing before reboot
values.description: Stops new reads while allowing active operations to complete before a server reboots.

values.label: Continued write delivery during quiescing
values.description: Continues sending writes to the quiescing replica so it does not fall arbitrarily behind.

values.label: Immediate reboot
values.description: Reboots without draining activity; rejected because it can interrupt long-running reads and clones.

values.label: Lost interrupted-clone progress
values.description: An interrupted large clone must restart elsewhere and loses progress already completed.

values.label: Replica catch-up load
values.description: Withheld writes would make a quiescing replica fall behind and create substantial recovery work.

values.label: Planned rolling reboot operations
values.description: Use sequential, bounded rolling reboots to test or perform changes while preserving service continuity.

values.label: Unplanned server reboot testing
values.description: Use random abrupt reboots as the primary test of single-node failure handling.

values.label: Unplanned server unplugging for retirement
values.description: Retire servers by abruptly unplugging them without quiescing active work.

clusters.name: Client Repository Materialization
clusters.description: How clients initially obtain repository objects and working data through virtualization, partial transfer, caching, or demand fetching.

relations.reading: Client Large-Repository Performance Strategy affects Packfile Lifecycle Management
relations.rationale: Client performance depends partly on pack counts, file-handle pressure, delta layout, and background maintenance efficiency.
