values.label: Two-phase consolidation and expiration
values.description: Separates pack creation and reference updates from deletion so cleanup occurs only after old packs are unreferenced.

values.label: Deferred unreferenced-pack deletion
values.description: Retains old packs until their objects have been redirected and no references remain.

values.label: Foreground-command continuity
values.description: Designs maintenance so foreground Git commands continue operating during repacking and expiration.

values.label: Loose-object cleanup
values.description: Maintenance removes accumulated loose objects to reduce storage and lookup overhead.

values.label: Single-pack full repacking
values.description: All repository data is rewritten into one packfile to reduce lookup overhead.

values.label: Background incremental repository maintenance
values.description: Perform repository cleanup and rewriting incrementally in background processes rather than blocking foreground commands.

values.label: Foreground automatic garbage collection
values.description: Run complete automatic garbage collection synchronously at the end of user commands.

values.label: Primary-only compaction scheduling
values.description: Schedule repository compaction on only the primary replica and propagate its results to peers.

values.label: WAL-propagated compaction events
values.description: Propagate compaction results through the WAL so replicas apply the same repository maintenance events.

values.label: S3 distribution of compacted packs
values.description: Distribute already-compacted packs from object storage instead of repacking independently on replicas.

values.label: Periodic write-ahead-log compaction
values.description: Compact the WAL periodically to bound restoration work as updates accumulate.

values.label: On-disk layout optimization for compaction
values.description: Optimize repository disk layout to reduce compaction impact on ingestion.

values.label: Replica-local repository repacking
values.description: Repack repositories independently on each replica.

values.label: Automatic Git garbage-collection disablement
values.description: Disable foreground automatic garbage collection and shift cleanup to background maintenance.

values.label: Unbounded packfile growth
values.description: Allows pack counts to grow without bound, creating file-handle scalability problems.

values.label: Pack-count and storage reduction
values.description: Deployment reduced repositories from thousands of packs and 150–200 GB to fewer than 100 packs and 30–50 GB.

values.label: Pack-index accumulation lookup cost
values.description: Accumulating packfiles increases the number of indexes Git must inspect and slows object lookup.

values.label: Foreground garbage-collection blocking
values.description: Foreground garbage collection blocks commands and can exhaust CPU and memory during repository rewrites.

values.label: Performance decay from disabled automatic collection
values.description: Avoid foreground collection but allow accumulated objects to gradually degrade Git performance.

values.label: Compaction-limited push throughput
values.description: Push throughput becomes bounded by on-disk compaction speed after WAL latency is reduced.

values.label: Replica failover from concurrent maintenance
values.description: Concurrent compaction on replicas can trigger repository failover and reduce availability.

selected_clusters.name: Repository Replication Layer
selected_clusters.description: Which system layer and mechanism performs repository replication across hosts.

relations.reading: Repository Replication Layer affects Replica Write Coordination Strategy
relations.rationale: The new documents state that geographic replica distance adds latency and constrains reference-update throughput.

relations.reading: Repository Replication Layer affects Replica Write Coordination Strategy
relations.rationale: The new documents state that geographic replica distance adds latency and constrains reference-update throughput.

relations.reading: Repository Replication Layer affects Replica Write Coordination Strategy
relations.rationale: The new documents state that geographic replica distance adds latency and constrains reference-update throughput.

values.label: DRBD block-level replication
values.description: Replication is performed below the application at the filesystem block level.

values.label: Co-located replica placement
values.description: Replicas are kept physically close to satisfy block-replication latency constraints.

values.label: Application-level Spokes replication
values.description: An application-level system replicates Git repositories and manages their copies across file servers.

values.label: Distant replica placement
values.description: Replicas are deliberately distributed across greater geographic distances despite added latency.

values.label: Git-and-rsync replication
values.description: Replication combines Git-aware operations with rsync for copying, repair, and rebalancing.

values.label: S3-backed write-ahead-log authority
values.description: Authoritative repository state is retained in durable object storage while hosts serve reconstructible working copies.

values.label: WAL-based repository provenance and replica rewind
values.description: The authoritative log records repository operations so states can be reconstructed, rewound, and fast-forwarded.

values.label: Optimistic UDP gossip replication
values.description: Exchange replica catch-up metadata through lossy gossip while retaining authoritative recovery from the WAL.

values.label: ETag-validated replica freshness
values.description: Validate replica currency against the WAL index before serving reads.

values.label: WAL-index catch-up before reads
values.description: Catch replicas up from a newer WAL index before serving fetches or clones.

values.label: S3-backed globally consistent reads
values.description: Use authoritative S3 state checks so replicas expose a consistent repository view despite message loss or topology changes.

values.label: Arbitrary replica-count scaling
values.description: Scale read-serving capacity by deploying an arbitrary number of consistent replicas.

values.label: Fully consistent replica cluster
values.description: Maintain full consistency across replicas while adding read and RPC serving capacity.

values.label: WAL-first storage design
values.description: Use the write-ahead log as the primary durability and replication foundation for repository updates.

values.label: S3 Express One Zone WAL storage
values.description: Use low-latency S3 Express One Zone as the WAL persistence layer for high push rates.

values.label: Batched WAL operations
values.description: Batch WAL writes to reduce object-store latency and sustain high push ingestion rates.

values.label: Single-S3-write-per-push model
values.description: Persist each push with one object-store write.

values.label: On-disk repository consensus authority
values.description: Repository copies on disk serve as the authoritative state for consensus and correctness.

values.label: Individually managed repository copies
values.description: Each repository copy is treated as a valuable, individually tracked operational asset.

values.label: Continuous repository checksum tracking
values.description: Replica checksums are continuously maintained to detect corruption in authoritative repository copies.

values.label: Per-update replica checksum validation
values.description: Replica logical contents are checked after each update using a checksum over reference-value state.

values.label: Incremental checksum maintenance
values.description: Replica checksums are updated incrementally instead of recomputed from scratch after every reference update.

values.label: From-scratch checksum recomputation
values.description: The checksum is fully recomputed for every update, imposing excessive cost in busy repositories.

values.label: Repository-operation burden at scale
values.description: Per-repository tracking, verification, corruption detection, and urgent repair create operational burden as scale grows.

selected_clusters.name: Repository Hosting Model
selected_clusters.description: Which collaboration and hosting model combines client decentralization with repository service centralization?

values.label: Distributed version-control model
values.description: Clients retain decentralized version-control capabilities while collaborating through hosted repositories.

values.label: Centralized repository hosting
values.description: Organizations rely on a central host for shared repository collaboration despite distributed client capabilities.

values.label: Hybrid distributed-client centralized-host architecture
values.description: Distributed client workflows such as offline work and delayed pushes operate against centralized repository hosting.

values.label: Distributed Git implementation
values.description: The hosting system itself distributes or modifies Git rather than retaining standard Git as the implementation boundary.

values.label: Git repository hosting difficulty
values.description: Hosting Git repositories creates substantial scalability and operational complexity.

selected_clusters.name: Repository Cache Materialization Strategy
selected_clusters.description: How repository state is cached, discarded, and reconstructed to balance local responsiveness, storage cost, and materialization work.

values.label: Local-disk repository warm cache
values.description: Hosts keep repositories as local working copies for efficient access without making local placement authoritative.

values.label: On-demand repository materialization
values.description: A missing repository is reconstructed from authoritative log state on the host that needs to serve it.

values.label: Idle-replica disk garbage collection
values.description: Remove inactive repository replicas from local disk to reduce retained storage.

values.label: On-demand replica rematerialization
values.description: Reconstruct an evicted repository replica from the WAL when demand returns.

criteria.name: Orthogonality
criteria.description: Every dimension is a distinct decision point: no two dimensions ask the same question, and no dimension's candidate decisions are really options of another dimension.
criteria.reason: Several dimensions are distinct, such as 26 Replica Write Authority and Quorum versus 17 Replica Commit Protocol, so they should not be merged. However, 21 Repository Placement and Routing combines physical placement with request/location selection and overlaps 9 Replica Repair and Redundancy Strategy (especially 9.7 Rendezvous-hashed repository placement) and 23 Replica Request Routing (23.6 Geo-replica read routing); split 21 into placement and routing questions, moving 9.7 to its placement part and the location-selection values to its routing part. 19 Git Object Distribution Consistency also overlaps 13 Repository Replication Layer because both contain replica distribution and synchronization choices; keep 19 focused on consistency policy and move mechanism choices such as 19.4–19.6 into 13. 24 Client Repository Materialization overlaps 25 Client Working-Tree Scope around virtualization and sparse/on-demand materialization; rename 24 to focus strictly on Git-object acquisition and move the working-environment virtualization choice 24.1 to 25.

criteria.name: Clarity
criteria.description: Dimension names and descriptions make the decision question clear, and value labels and descriptions make the alternatives distinguishable, so a reader could tell which dimension and value a passage about a design decision belongs to.
criteria.reason: Many dimensions have recognizable decision-oriented names and their values are described specifically, with accepted, rejected, mixed, and outcome statuses used consistently. However, several dimensions do not match the alternatives they contain. Dimension 21, "Repository Placement and Routing," includes outcomes such as 21.1 and 21.2 and only one actual routing-table alternative; rename it to reflect the included placement outcomes or reorganize those values under the dimensions whose decisions produce them. Dimension 19, "Git Object Distribution Consistency," similarly mixes failure effects (19.1–19.3) with distribution choices (19.4–19.6); revise its description and value grouping so each label clearly represents distribution/consistency alternatives or their explicit outcomes. Dimension 18, "Git Object Storage Format," does not cover 18.4 "Git-compatible native data format," which is a compatibility boundary rather than a physical format; rename the dimension to include representation and compatibility, or move 18.4 to an existing compatible dimension. Values in dimension 14, "Repository Hosting Model," are difficult to distinguish because 14.1, 14.2, and 14.3 substantially overlap; rewrite their descriptions to make the client/server boundary and hosting arrangement distinct. Dimension 26, "Replica Write Authority and Quorum," has overlapping choices such as majority quorum (26.1), durability-gated acceptance (26.4), synchronous multi-replica acceptance (26.5), and the consistency/partition policy (26.6); clarify each label as a separate alternative or consolidate the overlapping existing values.

criteria.name: Completeness
criteria.description: The taxonomy contains the major decision points implied by the use case, each with its main candidate decisions.
criteria.reason: The taxonomy represents the main scale-related decision areas with multiple alternatives: server object storage and access (18, 20), placement and replication (21, 26, 27, 17, 9, 13), failure and maintenance handling (22, 23, 5), packfile lifecycle (7), and client materialization and performance (24, 25, 11, 12). Most dimensions contain both adopted and rejected or mixed candidates rather than only one option. A minor gap is that very-many-user request/service scaling is only indirectly represented through replica routing and replication; reorganizing existing values from 20, 23, and 13 into a more explicit user-request serving decision would make that area easier to identify without adding content.

criteria.name: Use case alignment
criteria.description: Every dimension serves the stated use case; none is out of its scope.
criteria.reason: All dimensions are within the use case’s scope: they address architectural decisions for scaling Git hosting servers, repository storage and replication, failure and maintenance handling, and client-side materialization and performance. The taxonomy covers very many repositories and users through placement, routing, quorum, repair, caching, and packfile lifecycle decisions, and very large repositories through sparse working trees, partial cloning, demand fetching, and Git performance mechanisms. No dimension is clearly outside the stated server/client scalability and lifecycle context.

criteria.name: No catch-alls
criteria.description: No dimension or value is a vague catch-all ('Other', 'Miscellaneous', 'General', 'Other approaches').
criteria.reason: Several dimensions are catch-all buckets rather than focused decision points. Dimension 11, "Client Git Performance Mechanisms," groups tracing, commit graphs, sparse checkout, filesystem monitoring, index formats, and status behavior; split it into focused existing-content dimensions for repository maintenance/graph decisions and working-tree/index inspection decisions. Dimension 12, "Client Repository Management Strategy," combines Scalar configuration, background fetching, maintenance, logging, and Git-native transition; split those into management-layer and background-maintenance decisions. Dimension 13, "Repository Replication Layer," mixes replication placement, WAL authority, gossip, freshness checks, scaling, and checksum validation; split it into replication mechanism and replica-integrity/authority decisions. Dimension 20, "Repository Access Mechanism," combines RPC, filesystems, protocols, caching, local NVMe, HTTP hosting, and reference databases; split server-side storage/access from client or protocol transfer alternatives. Dimension 9, "Replica Repair and Redundancy Strategy," combines repair, reconstruction, replication factor, placement, rack geography, and elastic allocation; split repair/reconstruction from redundancy and placement decisions. These broad buckets make the taxonomy retain multiple unrelated alternatives under one question.

criteria.name: Axis vs. value
criteria.description: Each dimension is a decision point with alternatives, not a single option presented as a dimension; each value is an option, not a sub-topic.
criteria.reason: The taxonomy contains some valid decision dimensions, such as 22 Failure Detection Strategy and 23 Replica Request Routing, but many dimensions combine multiple broader decisions or treat mechanisms and constraints as options. Dimension 18 Git Object Storage Format mixes representation, compatibility, and storage placement; split it into separate existing decision questions and move 18.4 and 18.5 accordingly. Dimension 20 Repository Access Mechanism mixes access protocols, server placement, caching, and reference storage; split those decision points and move 20.6, 20.7, and 20.9 to the relevant placement or reference-storage dimension. Dimension 9 Replica Repair and Redundancy Strategy combines repair, replication factor, placement, and geographic failure domains; move 9.7–9.9 to 21 Repository Placement and Routing and keep repair/redundancy alternatives together. Dimension 17 Replica Commit Protocol contains implementation steps such as 17.5 Pre-acquired reference locks, 17.6 Reference-update precondition validation, and 17.7 Atomic reference-update rollback rather than alternative answers to one decision; reorganize them under the actual commit-protocol alternatives or drop them as non-decision values. Dimension 27 Reference Write Scheduling includes forces or outcomes such as 27.1 Reference-update latency budget and 27.2 Read-preserving write optimization alongside scheduling alternatives; retain 27.3 and 27.4 as the scheduling choices and remove or relocate the non-option entries.

criteria.name: One decision point
criteria.description: Each dimension is a single decision point: all its candidate decisions are alternative answers to one question, rather than a broad topic bundling several questions. Where the use case names quality attributes or forces, dimensions whose choice is driven by recognizable quality attributes or trade-offs are preferred (quality-attribute grounding).
criteria.reason: The output correctly uses JSON, distinguishes outcomes from candidate decisions, and grounds many choices in scale concerns such as latency, availability, storage cost, and client performance. However, most dimensions are broad bundles of different decision questions. Dimension 20, "Repository Access Mechanism," mixes RPC interfaces, filesystem replication, local storage, caching, protocol format, and reference databases; split it into interface and storage/replication decisions, moving 20.4 to 15 and 20.5 to 18. Dimension 26, "Replica Write Authority and Quorum," combines leadership, quorum, durability, consistency, and arbitrary-server acceptance; split these into at least a write-authority question (26.2, 26.3, 26.7) and a write-acceptance/quorum question (26.1, 26.4, 26.5, 26.6). Dimension 17, "Replica Commit Protocol," similarly mixes transaction semantics, locking, commit protocol, WAL updates, and replica scope; split the transaction/validation choices from coordination/locking and move WAL-specific content to 13. Dimension 24, "Client Repository Materialization," combines initial object selection, virtualization, on-demand fetching, cache deployment, and Scalar/GVFS adoption; split initial materialization (24.1-24.5, 24.11) from cache strategy (24.6-24.8), moving service-management alternatives toward 12. Dimension 9, "Replica Repair and Redundancy Strategy," mixes repair, replica count, placement, geographic distribution, and elastic allocation; split those groups while retaining at least two candidate values per resulting decision. Dimension 27 also mixes constraints (27.1-27.2) with scheduling mechanisms (27.3-27.4), so it should be split into those two two-valued decision points.

criteria.name: Rejected-alternative handling
criteria.description: For each candidate decision, the taxonomy makes clear whether sources adopted it, rejected it, or disagree (status 'accepted', 'rejected' or 'mixed'); a rejected alternative is never presented as adopted; each candidate decision appears once with its stance; outcomes (status 'outcome') are kept apart from candidate decisions.
criteria.reason: Most values use valid statuses, and many rejected options and outcomes are described consistently. However, Repository Placement and Routing value 21.1 is an alternative placement choice mislabeled as an outcome; rename it to express the resulting availability/performance limitations or reclassify it as a rejected candidate. Replica Request Routing values 23.6 and 23.7 duplicate nearest-replica routing under accepted and outcome statuses; merge 23.7 into 23.6 and retain the candidate decision. Several mixed candidates are described as straightforward adoption: 24.1 Virtualized filesystem, 24.9 GVFS under insufficient cache infrastructure, 26.4 Durability-gated write acceptance, and 26.7 Arbitrary-server push acceptance. Revise those descriptions to explicitly state the sources' disagreement or conditional adoption rather than presenting each as simply used.

criteria.name: Dimensional coverage
criteria.description: Every sampled passage that discusses a design decision can be placed under at least one decision point (dimension) of the taxonomy.
criteria.reason: All decision-bearing passages can be placed under at least one taxonomy dimension. Scalar choices in s04_p01, s04_p02, s05_p04, s05_p09, s05_p11, and s05_p12 map to client materialization, working-tree scope, Git performance, management, and packfile lifecycle dimensions. Spokes decisions in s02_p01, s02_p02, s02_p03, s02_p04, s02_p06, s03_p07, s03_p08, s03_p09, and s03_p02 map to replication, quorum, commit protocol, routing, scheduling, repair, and planned maintenance dimensions. Architectural alternatives in s01_p03, s01_p04, s01_p05, and s01_p11 are also represented. No decision-bearing passage is unplaceable, so there are no taxonomy issues to fix.

criteria.reason: The taxonomy names nearly all adopted and rejected options across the passages, including background Scalar maintenance, partial working trees, three-phase commit, quorum writes, quiescing, rolling reboots, rack zones, and WAL-based replication. Missing or insufficiently explicit options are: add accepted value 'Git partial clone' to dimension 24 'Client Repository Materialization', supported by s04_p01 and s04_p02; add accepted value 'Cone-mode sparse-checkout' to dimension 25 'Client Working-Tree Scope', supported by s05_p04; add accepted value 'Graceful replica retirement by removing active membership while continuing service' to dimension 5 'Planned Maintenance Continuity', supported by s03_p09; and add accepted value 'Replica-based distributed locking' to dimension 17 'Replica Commit Protocol', supported by s02_p03.

criteria.name: Orthogonality
criteria.description: Every dimension is a distinct decision point: no two dimensions ask the same question, and no dimension's candidate decisions are really options of another dimension.
criteria.reason: The dimensions are largely distinct decision questions: object representation (1), repository access (2), replica consistency and repair (3), failure detection and routing (4), maintenance continuity (5), client performance (6), and packfile lifecycle management (7). Although dimensions 1 and 7 both discuss packfiles, they address different questions—representation/transfer versus consolidation and deletion—so they should not be merged. Similarly, dimensions 3–5 concern related availability mechanisms but distinguish consistency and repair, failure detection/routing, and planned maintenance. The only minor concern is that dimensions 1, 3, 4, and 6 combine closely related subtopics, but the output does not present a clear pair of dimensions asking the same question.

criteria.name: Clarity
criteria.description: Dimension names and descriptions make the decision question clear, and value labels and descriptions make the alternatives distinguishable, so a reader could tell which dimension and value a passage about a design decision belongs to.
criteria.reason: The taxonomy generally provides clear decision-oriented dimensions and distinguishable descriptions, especially for replica repair (3), failure routing (4), maintenance continuity (5), and packfile lifecycle (7). Revise dimension 1, "Git Object Representation Strategy," because 1.1 "Packfile-based object representation" and 1.2 "Delta-compressed packfile objects" overlap as accepted packfile representations; merge them or explicitly make one the broader representation choice and retain 1.7 only for the transfer-format choice. criteria.name: Completeness
criteria.description: The taxonomy contains the major decision points implied by the use case, each with its main candidate decisions.
criteria.reason: All major decision areas evident in the use case are represented by dimensions with multiple alternatives: server object representation and storage access (1, 2), replication and repair (3), failure routing (4), planned maintenance (5), client support for very large repositories (6), and packfile lifecycle management (7). criteria.name: Use case alignment

criteria.name: No catch-alls
criteria.description: No dimension or value is a vague catch-all ('Other', 'Miscellaneous', 'General', 'Other approaches').
criteria.reason: Most dimensions are focused decisions with explicit accepted, rejected, and outcome values, and no generic values such as “Other” or “Miscellaneous.” The main catch-all is dimension 6, “Client Large-Repository Performance Strategy,” whose description combines virtualization, Git-native improvements, Scalar configuration, tracing, and maintenance automation. Split this existing content into focused dimensions, such as how client access is virtualized (values 6.1, 6.2, and 6.4) versus how performance capabilities are implemented and maintained (values 6.3 and 6.5–6.11).

criteria.name: Axis vs. value
criteria.description: Each dimension is a decision point with alternatives, not a single option presented as a dimension; each value is an option, not a sub-topic.
criteria.reason: Several dimensions combine separate decisions or contain values that are sub-decisions rather than alternatives. In dimension 1, value 1.2 is a refinement of 1.1, while 1.7 is a separate protocol-transfer decision; fold 1.2 into 1.1 and separate or relocate 1.7. Dimension 3 combines quorum/ordering, rollback, replica removal and repair, and replication factor; split these existing values into distinct decision dimensions. Dimension 4 combines failure detection with request routing; retain 4.2–4.4 as detection choices and move 4.1 into the repository-access/routing decision. Dimension 6 is an umbrella for virtualization, Git-native performance, tracing, Scalar scope and individual optimizations; split the virtualization choices 6.1, 6.2 and 6.4 from the Scalar/Git-management choices and fold tactical values 6.5–6.7 into the relevant strategy descriptions. Dimension 7 likewise presents lifecycle steps such as 7.2–7.5 as peer alternatives even though they are components of one consolidation process; reorganize them under the lifecycle strategy while retaining 7.1 as the actual strategy choice. criteria.name: One decision point

Where the use case names quality attributes or forces, dimensions whose choice is driven by recognizable quality attributes or trade-offs are preferred (quality-attribute grounding).

Dimension 2 mixes RPC access, storage substrate/replication, and caching; separate access path values 2.1–2.2 from storage choices 2.3–2.4 and place 2.5 with the access/cache question. Dimension 4 mixes failure detection with routing; separate detection values 4.2–4.4 and move routing value 4.1 into the existing access/routing decision. Dimension 1 mixes object representation with protocol transfer: 1.1–1.4 should answer representation, while 1.7 needs merging into an existing packfile/transfer decision rather than remaining in the same broad topic.
